message.content:
Harden Nxeon's Valheim game servers against crossplay breaking after restarts. Owner-approved scope (2026-10-07): turn OFF the daily scheduled restart by default, and build the self-healing layers.

BACKGROUND (real incident 2026-10-07): customer server TERRAHEIM (Server id cmtsspvu10jf1hlo7x798z354, VM 119 on node-3, image lloesche/valheim-server, BEPINEX=true, CROSSPLAY=true). The lloesche image's default RESTART_CRON ("10 5 * * *") + RESTART_IF_IDLE restarted valheim-server at 05:10 UTC. During shutdown it logged "Failed to send, suspend TX on playfab/...", so the old PlayFab lobby likely wasn't cleaned up. On boot: `Sending PlayFab login request (attempt 2)`, `Session "Nxeon" registered with join code 187714`, then an exception `at ZPlayFabMatchmaking.OnCheckJoinCodeSuccess (PlayFab.MultiplayerModels.FindLobbiesResult result)`, and never the healthy line `Session "<name>" with join code <code> and IP <ip>:<port> is active with N player(s)`. Nobody could join for ~45 min. A container restart fixed it (the healthy line appeared). Also note: with CROSSPLAY on, port 2456 isn't bound in the guest (verify-game-provision flags it), which is expected for crossplay; don't treat it as a failure for crossplay servers.

Codebase: /opt/nxeon (Next.js 15 + Prisma + worker in worker/). Game config schema: lib/game-config.ts (Valheim family, CROSSPLAY, env passthrough). Game config is applied by GAME_CONFIG jobs (worker). Guest access: lib/ssh-exec.ts withServerSsh/exec. Health tooling: scripts/verify-game-provision.ts. Docs: docs/DOCUMENTATION.md.

BUILD
1. **No daily restart by default.** For Valheim servers, set the container env so the image never restarts on a schedule (RESTART_CRON empty/disabled; check the lloesche docs/entrypoint for the exact way: inspect the image on a real guest read-only, e.g. `docker exec valheim cat /usr/local/bin/valheim-bootstrap`). Keep update-triggered restarts (the image's updater restarts only when a Valheim update exists and the server is idle). Add an optional per-server "Scheduled restart" setting in the customer game panel (off by default; time picker in the server's local region time; skipped if players online). Also check whether the same default restart exists for other game families the platform runs on lloesche-like images, and report (don't change other games without saying so).
2. **Crossplay health check + auto-heal** (worker sweep, e.g. every 1–2 min for running Valheim servers with CROSSPLAY on, cheap: tail the log since last check): healthy = the "is active with" line seen after the latest start; broken = OnCheckJoinCodeSuccess/PlayFab exception after a start, or no "is active" line within ~3 min of a start, or repeated "PlayFab network error" with 0 players for N minutes. On broken: restart valheim-server ONCE automatically (via the normal GAME_POWER/GAME_CONFIG job path, audited), recheck, and if still broken raise an admin alert (existing admin notification mechanism). Rate-limit restarts (never loop). Record state so the panel can show it.
3. **Clean shutdown**: before any platform-initiated stop/restart of a Valheim crossplay server, give the game a graceful shutdown long enough for PlayFab unregister (check what the image does on SIGTERM / supervisorctl stop and the container stop timeout; raise the timeout if it kills the process before "Unregister PlayFab server" completes). Verify on a THROWAWAY server.
4. **Join code + status in the panel**: show the current crossplay join code (parsed from the log line "registered with join code NNNNNN" / "is active with") and a live badge: Crossplay healthy / Reconnecting / Needs attention, plus "players join with code X, or by IP host:port". Works in dark and light themes (use portal tokens, no hard-coded dark colours).
5. **Memory watch (light)**: if a Valheim guest's available memory stays under a threshold for a sustained period, show the customer a "restart recommended" hint and log it for admins (no automatic restart for this).
6. **Rollout script for existing servers** (DRY RUN by default): lists every existing Valheim server and what will change (env RESTART_CRON off). With --apply it queues the config change ONLY for servers with 0 players online, skipping busy ones (so the container recreate never kicks players). Do NOT run --apply against customer servers yourself; leave it for the parent/owner. Also a read-only report of every crossplay Valheim server's current health (is it in the broken state right now?) and include the list in your report.

TESTING: provision a THROWAWAY Valheim server for real to prove the crossplay flow, the clean shutdown and the auto-heal. Use the owner's preview account nicholas.sj.albanese@gmail.com (user id cmrztujaw0002hlazl58i3lsi), placing the order the same way the platform does (lib/game-order.ts placeGameOrder; the account has wallet credit), then tear it down afterwards with a DELETE job. Never touch customer servers other than read-only checks. Never reuse VM IDs (the platform allocates them). Don't email customers.

RULES (hard)
- Worktree off main: `git -C /opt/nxeon worktree add /tank/nxeon-wt-valheimheal -b fix/valheim-crossplay-selfheal main`. node_modules: your own directory of symlinks into /tank/nxeon-wt-release2/node_modules with your own generated Prisma client; never commit it; NEVER `git add -A`.
- Never edit/build in /opt/nxeon. Heavy commands as `flock /root/.nxeon-build.lock nice -n 15 ionice -c3 env NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=3072 ...`. Never pkill by pattern. Don't deploy or merge to main; schema changes additive only.
- Tests (repo uses `tsx --test`, node:test + node:assert, NOT vitest), tsc clean, docs updated.

FINAL REPORT (concise): what changed per layer, what was verified for real on the throwaway server vs not, the crossplay-health report of current customer servers, the rollout script usage, commits, and owner decisions.

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions. Claude publishes an artifact for apps, sites, dashboards and games, and whenever the person asks for an artifact or for an HTML or Markdown page to view or share. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. A page declares these through the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of this would make the page more useful, Claude must load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code.** Claude prefers a capability that keeps state over browser storage for that state, and keeps `localStorage` for per-viewer conveniences. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Claude always authors the page as `.html`, and publishes a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly asks for one. When the person shares a Markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, Claude builds an HTML page from its content, keeping its substance and designing the page as it would any other artifact rather than transcribing the Markdown one to one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB work, but each artifact has its own origin and what a page stores lives only in that viewer's browser. It survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices or Claude. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform

Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).

## Architecture

- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).

## Portals & design system

**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.

- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).

- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).

- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.

- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).

## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session

`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.

1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.

If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).

## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)

- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.

## Conventions

- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.

## Documentation — keep it current (required)

- **Every change, fix, or addition MUST update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` in the same commit.** Add a dated bullet to §15 (Change history) and edit any section the change affects (data model, subsystems, feature catalog, integrations, roadmap, etc.). A commit that changes behaviour without touching the docs is incomplete.
- Keep `ROADMAP.md` in sync too: check off / move the item you completed.
- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` is the single source of truth. The public mirror at `https://revsports.ca/docs` is regenerated from it with `node scripts/publish-docs.mjs` (zero-dep markdown→styled-HTML renderer → `/var/www/nxeon-docs/index.html`) — run that after editing the doc so the hosted page matches. The `/docs` nginx location lives in `scripts/configure-domains.sh` so it survives vhost regeneration.
- The claude.ai artifact webpage (`https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9b0c97f5-4c34-4f89-bee9-b5a80eb23892`) can only be updated from an interactive Claude Code session (headless/cron runs can't reach it) — that refresh is best-effort, the repo doc + `/docs` page are authoritative.

## Commands

- Typecheck: `npx tsc --noEmit` (always, before a build)
- Build: `npm run build` (must pass before restarting services)
- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
- Worker logs: `journalctl -u nxeon-worker -f`
- E2E test: `npx tsx scripts/e2e-test.ts` (orders a real VM; delete it afterwards via a DELETE job)
- Admin credentials: `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`

## Domains & TLS

- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
- Secure cookies are on (`COOKIE_SECURE=1`) now that real HTTPS exists. Stripe webhook is live at `https://BASE_DOMAIN/api/stripe/webhook`.

## Environments

- **Production**: `/opt/nxeon`, DB `nxeon`, services `nxeon-web` (port 3000) + `nxeon-worker`, nginx port 80, VPS pools IP 10.20.0.100–250 / SSH ports 20000–29999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD`. Public: http://51.79.162.96
- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
- Instance differences are driven entirely by `.env` (NXEON_ENV, NXEON_COOKIE_NAME, NXEON_NAT_CHAIN, NXEON_TAG, NXEON_IP_START/END, NXEON_SSH_PORT_START/END, NXEON_CRED_FILE, PORT, APP_URL) — the code is identical.
- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.

## Safety rules

- NEVER touch VMIDs 9000–9999 (templates) except to add new templates.
- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.
- Never `qm destroy` a VM that has a `Server` row — always go through a DELETE job.
- Never `pkill -f` by pattern on this box — kill by port PID or systemd unit instead (a pattern match has restarted live production before).
- Do not commit `.env`. Do not print the Proxmox token into logs or docs.
- Always `git commit` working states; never leave the tree broken — services restart from this directory.

setup_crontab() {
    local crontab
    crontab=$(mktemp)

    { echo "SERVER_PUBLIC=$SERVER_PUBLIC"; \
        echo "SERVER_PORT=$SERVER_PORT"; \
        echo "STATUS_HTTP_HTDOCS=$STATUS_HTTP_HTDOCS"; } >> "$crontab"

    if [ "$BACKUPS" = true ] && [ -n "$BACKUPS_CRON" ] && [ "$BACKUPS_INTERVAL" = "315360000" ]; then

        echo "$BACKUPS_CRON [ -f \"$valheim_backup_pidfile\" ] && kill -HUP \$(cat $valheim_backup_pidfile)" >> "$crontab"
    fi

    if [ -n "$UPDATE_CRON" ] && [ "$UPDATE_INTERVAL" = "315360000" ]; then
        debug "Creating cron to check for updates using schedule $UPDATE_CRON"
        echo "$UPDATE_CRON [ -f \"$valheim_updater_pidfile\" ] && kill -HUP \$(cat $valheim_updater_pidfile)" >> "$crontab"

    if [ -n "$RESTART_CRON" ]; then
        debug "Creating cron to restart valheim-server using schedule $RESTART_CRON"

    fi

    # Via stdin: busybox would open a file argument as valheim, who can't read it
    if ! crontab -u valheim - < "$crontab"; then
        error "Failed to install crontab - scheduled backups, updates and restarts won't run"

run_server() {
    pre_server_run_hook
    info "Running Valheim Server"
    debug "Server config is name: $SERVER_NAME, port: $SERVER_PORT/udp, world: $WORLD_NAME, public: $SERVER_PUBLIC, mod: $mod_name"
    update_server_status starting

    chmod +x "$valheim_server"

    # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2016
    setsid env \
        SERVER_LD_PRELOAD="$SERVER_LD_PRELOAD" \
        LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$LD_LIBRARY_PATH" \
        DOORSTOP_ENABLED="$DOORSTOP_ENABLED" \
        DOORSTOP_TARGET_ASSEMBLY="$DOORSTOP_TARGET_ASSEMBLY" \
        bash -c \
            'export LD_LIBRARY_PATH DOORSTOP_ENABLED DOORSTOP_TARGET_ASSEMBLY; LD_PRELOAD=$SERVER_LD_PRELOAD exec "$0" "$@"' \
            "$valheim_server" -nographics -batchmode -name "$SERVER_NAME" -port "$SERVER_PORT" -world "$WORLD_NAME" -public "$SERVER_PUBLIC" \
            "${valheim_server_args[@]}" $SERVER_ARGS > >(filter) 2>&1 &

    valheim_server_pid=$!

    unset LD_LIBRARY_PATH
    unset LD_PRELOAD
    echo $valheim_server_pid > "$valheim_server_pidfile"

    ensure_permissions_after_start &
    permissions_wait_pid=$!
    wait_for_server_listening &
    wait_for_server_listening_pid=$!

    wait $valheim_server_pid
    debug "Valheim server with PID $valheim_server_pid stopped"
    update_server_status stopped
    post_server_run_hook

    cleanup
    post_server_shutdown_hook
    info "Shutdown complete"
    exit 0
}


cleanup() {
    if [ -n "${permissions_wait_pid:-}" ] && [ -d "/proc/$permissions_wait_pid" ]; then
        kill -TERM $permissions_wait_pid
    fi
    if [ -n "${wait_for_server_listening_pid:-}" ] && [ -d "/proc/$wait_for_server_listening_pid" ]; then
        kill -TERM $wait_for_server_listening_pid
    fi
    clear_lock "$valheim_server_pidfile"
}

elif [ "$BEPINEX" = true ]; then
    cd "$bepinex_install_path" || fatal "Could not cd $bepinex_install_path"

    export DOORSTOP_ENABLED=1

main() {
    wait_for_server_download
    run_server
}

#shellcheck disable=SC2317
shutdown() {
    debug "Received signal to shut down valheim-server"
    update_server_status stopping
    if [ "$valheim_server_pid" -eq -1 ]; then
        debug "Valheim server is not running yet - aborting startup"
        update_server_status stopped
        exit
    fi
    pre_server_shutdown_hook
    info "Shutting down Valheim server with PID $valheim_server_pid"
    kill -INT -"$valheim_server_pid"
    shutdown_timeout=$(($(date +%s)+timeout))
    while [ -d "/proc/$valheim_server_pid" ]; do
        if [ "$(date +%s)" -gt "$shutdown_timeout" ]; then
            shutdown_timeout=$(($(date +%s)+timeout))
            warn "Timeout while waiting for server to shut down - sending SIG$kill_signal to PGID $valheim_server_pid"
            kill -"$kill_signal" -"$valheim_server_pid"
            case "$kill_signal" in
                INT)
                    kill_signal=TERM
                    ;;
                *)
                    kill_signal=KILL
            esac
        fi
        debug "Waiting for Valheim Server with PID $valheim_server_pid to shut down"
        sleep 6
    done
}


#shellcheck disable=SC2317
pre_server_shutdown_hook() {
    if [ -n "$PRE_SERVER_SHUTDOWN_HOOK" ]; then
        info "Running pre server shutdown hook: $PRE_SERVER_SHUTDOWN_HOOK"
        eval "$PRE_SERVER_SHUTDOWN_HOOK"
    fi
}


post_server_shutdown_hook() {
    if [ -n "$POST_SERVER_SHUTDOWN_HOOK" ]; then
        info "Running post server shutdown hook: $POST_SERVER_SHUTDOWN_HOOK"
        eval "$POST_SERVER_SHUTDOWN_HOOK"
    fi
}

content.content:
# Scheduled Operation Environment Variables

Based on the documentation, here are the relevant cron-related variables:

**Update Variables:**
- `UPDATE_CRON` - Default: (not set/empty)
- `UPDATE_CHECK_PLAYERS` - Default: `false`

**Restart Variables:**
- `RESTART_CRON` - Default: (not set/empty)
- `RESTART_CHECK_PLAYERS` - Default: `false`

**Backup Variables:**
- `BACKUP_CRON` - Default: (not set/empty)
- `BACKUP_MAX_COUNT` - Default: `0`

## Default Behavior

No, the image does **not** restart the server on a schedule by default. All three cron variables (`UPDATE_CRON`, `RESTART_CRON`, and `BACKUP_CRON`) have empty default values, meaning no automatic scheduling occurs unless explicitly configured. You must set these environment variables with a cron expression (e.g., `*/30 * * * *`) to enable scheduled operations.

# Automatic Reboot Environment Variables

Based on the documentation, here are the automatic reboot scheduling variables:

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `AUTO_REBOOT_ENABLED` | `false` | Activates automatic reboots |
| `AUTO_REBOOT_CRON_EXPRESSION` | `0 0 * * *` | Sets reboot schedule (midnight daily by timezone) |
| `AUTO_REBOOT_WARN_MINUTES` | `5` | Warning time before reboot occurs |
| `AUTO_REBOOT_EVEN_IF_PLAYERS_ONLINE` | `false` | Determines if server reboots with active players |

**Does it restart on schedule by default?** No. The server does not automatically reboot unless you explicitly set `AUTO_REBOOT_ENABLED=true`. When enabled, the default schedule is "everynight at midnight according to the timezone set with TZ."

. /usr/local/etc/valheim/defaults
. /usr/local/etc/valheim/common


main() {
    apply_permissions
    configure_timezone
    setup_syslog
    setup_supervisor_http_server
    setup_status_http_server
    pre_supervisor_hook
    setup_crontab
    exec /usr/bin/tini -- /usr/local/bin/supervisord -c /usr/local/etc/supervisord.conf
}


apply_permissions() {
    info "Setting uid:gid of valheim to $PUID:$PGID"
    groupmod -g "${PGID}" -o valheim
    #usermod -u "${PUID}" -o -g valheim valheim
    sed -i -E "s/^(valheim:x):[0-9]+:[0-9]+:(.*)/\\1:$PUID:$PGID:\\2/" /etc/passwd

    mkdir -p /var/run/valheim
    touch "$SERVER_STATUS_FILE"

    chown -R valheim:valheim \
        /config \
        /opt/valheim \
        /opt/steamcmd \
        /home/valheim \
        /var/run/valheim \
        "$SERVER_STATUS_FILE"
    chgrp valheim /usr/local/etc/supervisord.conf
}


configure_timezone() {
    export TZ
    if [ ! -f "/usr/share/zoneinfo/$TZ" ]; then
        warn "Unknown timezone $TZ - defaulting to Etc/UTC"
        TZ="Etc/UTC"
    fi
    ln -snf "/usr/share/zoneinfo/$TZ" /etc/localtime
    echo "$TZ" > /etc/timezone
    info "Setting timezone $TZ"
}


setup_syslog() {

# Install valheim's crontab as root, so busybox crontab needn't be suid
setup_crontab() {
    local crontab
    crontab=$(mktemp)

    { echo "SERVER_PUBLIC=$SERVER_PUBLIC"; \
        echo "SERVER_PORT=$SERVER_PORT"; \
        echo "STATUS_HTTP_HTDOCS=$STATUS_HTTP_HTDOCS"; } >> "$crontab"

    if [ "$BACKUPS" = true ] && [ -n "$BACKUPS_CRON" ] && [ "$BACKUPS_INTERVAL" = "315360000" ]; then

        echo "$BACKUPS_CRON [ -f \"$valheim_backup_pidfile\" ] && kill -HUP \$(cat $valheim_backup_pidfile)" >> "$crontab"
    fi

    if [ -n "$UPDATE_CRON" ] && [ "$UPDATE_INTERVAL" = "315360000" ]; then
        debug "Creating cron to check for updates using schedule $UPDATE_CRON"
        echo "$UPDATE_CRON [ -f \"$valheim_updater_pidfile\" ] && kill -HUP \$(cat $valheim_updater_pidfile)" >> "$crontab"
    fi

    if [ -n "$RESTART_CRON" ]; then
        debug "Creating cron to restart valheim-server using schedule $RESTART_CRON"
        if [ "$RESTART_IF_IDLE" = true ]; then
            echo "$RESTART_CRON $cmd_valheim_is_idle && $cmd_supervisorctl restart valheim-server" >> "$crontab"

        fi

    if ! crontab -u valheim - < "$crontab"; then

content.thinking:
I'm starting on a pure health-checking module for Valheim, designing flexible regex patterns to parse log lines that I'll refine once I see actual log output. For reading logs, I'm planning to pull from journalctl for the valheim.service unit, bounded by a time cursor and line limit to capture recent container stdout.

I'm thinking through edge cases: a watch cursor based on the last processed timestamp could miss lines with identical timestamps, which seems negligible. The trickier issue is the first sweep — if the container started hours or days ago, a short time window won't capture the actual server start event, so I need to decide whether to look back further or rely on docker's container start metadata instead.

Now I'm sketching the state machine for tracking server health: persisting timestamps for the last start, last active, last registration/join code, and last error, plus counters for network errors since the last active event. The classification logic checks these timestamps in order — crossplay disabled, no data yet, errors after the latest start with no subsequent activity (marking it broken), or activity after the latest start (marking it healthy).

For the "starting" vs "broken" distinction, I'm weighing a timeout window — maybe 3-4 minutes after the start marker to account for BepInEx's initial boot and download time — before flagging a stalled session as broken due to no crossplay session appearing. I'm also second-guessing whether the "is active with" line only prints once per session, and whether some game versions might skip printing it altogether, which would break this detection approach.

To guard against false positives causing unnecessary restarts, I want to cap auto-heal attempts: only one heal per start cycle, escalate to alert if it's still broken afterward, and hold off further heals until a healthy state is confirmed, plus an overall limit of two heals per 24 hours. For the registration case, I'll require seeing the active line specifically, since that's what matched the actual incident pattern. For the UI badges, I'm mapping the internal states down to three simple labels — healthy, reconnecting (covering starting/reconnecting/healing), and needs attention (covering broken/alerted) — with unknown states still needing a mapping decision.

Now I'm working out the healing state machine: if a server is broken with no players and no heal attempted yet this episode, restart it and record timestamps; if it's already been healed once this episode and is still broken, fire a single alert rather than healing repeatedly. A clean healthy signal resets the episode and clears any pending alert, and I'm capping total heals to three within a rolling 24-hour window using a stored timestamp history, falling back to alerting once that cap is hit. I also need to handle the case where a heal-triggered restart leads to broken again — comparing timestamps to detect this and alert rather than loop forever.

I'm also adding a separate memory watchdog that reads guest memory from /proc/meminfo, flags sustained low availability over 15 minutes, uses hysteresis to clear the alert, and logs a one-time audit entry per episode for admins. Sweep cadence differs by server type — every 60 seconds for crossplay servers with memory checks piggybacking, versus a lighter memory-only check interval for non-crossplay servers.

I'm also thinking through the gamePower flow: skip the port-check wait for crossplay servers since their sessions register differently, instead notifying the user that status will appear in the panel, and adjusting probeGameRuntime's logic accordingly for crossplay cases.

I should revisit verify-game-provision.ts, where error 2456 is flagged, so crossplay servers aren't incorrectly treated as a failure there. I also need to handle scheduled restarts through GameSchedule, factoring in timezone and the skipIfPlayers option.

The GAME_POWER restart path uses a clean shutdown, which is fine as is. For the time picker, I should resolve the server's local region time from server.node.region into a regionTimezone value. Now I'm ready to start writing lib/valheim-health.ts.

content.thinking:
My test scripts need the ValheimWatch table, but prod DB doesn't have it yet, and creating it there would count as a deploy action I'm supposed to avoid. I need another way to test the sweep logic without touching prod schema.

I can keep the sweep logic pure and separable — a function that checks a server against its previous state and returns a decision — with a test harness that stores state in memory or a file instead of the DB, while still letting heal actions flow through the real GAME_POWER job path. Now I'm writing a read-only SSH probe script to check the Docker container's running state, start time, environment variables, memory, and recent logs, with logic to resolve the correct systemd unit name across possible hints like valheim or valheim-server.

For containers without a systemd unit (older setups relying on Docker restart policy), I need a fallback that pulls logs via `docker logs` with RFC3339 timestamps, which means writing a second parser just for that format. I'm also thinking through RESTART_CRON detection via env grep, and how to bound the first log read window using container start time versus a 6-hour lookback, capped at 3000 lines — though I still need to verify whether Valheim periodically logs an "active" heartbeat line to handle the case where the last restart was further back than that window.

I'm setting concurrency to 4 parallel server checks, then for each server: pulling the previous memory row, parsing new events since the cursor, folding them into updated memory, classifying crossplay state, and deciding whether to heal or alert. Healing triggers a restart job with audit logging and heal history tracking, while alerting notifies admins — and I'm considering whether to add a customer-facing in-app notification on top of what the power job itself already announces.

I also want to add safeguards: skip the check if there's already a job in flight for that server or if the server isn't meant to be running, and respect env flags like VALHEIM_WATCH and VALHEIM_CROSSPLAY_AUTOHEAL to disable sweeping or restrict to alert-only mode. I'm planning to structure the core logic as a pure, testable `evaluateWatch` function, with probe script generation and output parsing split into their own reusable lib functions.

This should cause login requests to repeatedly fail without the server ever reaching an active state, which is the real failure case I need to simulate. The background sweep loop with --act is already running, so I'll just let it continue and switch to this new blocking approach now rather than stopping it first.

## Game server control panel — power, live console/RCON, restarts, worlds

**What it does.** A **Manage** tab (game servers only, injected after Overview in
`components/customer/ServerTabs.tsx`) giving a Pterodactyl/Nitrado-style panel over the customer's own
game VM, entirely on the platform's existing SSH:

- **Power** — start/stop/restart the *game service* (systemd unit), distinct from VM power. `GAME_POWER`
  job → `worker/game-control.ts gamePower`, which resolves the unit from per-family hints and checks the
  `systemctl` exit code (NXGP markers, same "a clean SSH exit proves nothing" discipline as
  `worker/game-update.ts`). In the hero (`components/customer/gamepanel/v2/GameHero.tsx`) the buttons
  are driven by `usePowerGuard` (added 2026-09-30): locked from the click until the real `GAME_POWER`
  job ends — which can be seconds or, with `powerStartTimeoutMs` and up to 3 worker attempts, many
  minutes — with "Starting… 1m 12s" / "attempt 2" shown from real job data, the status pill reading the
  in-flight action, a success/failure line when it ends, and a 5 s cooldown after. `gamePower` enqueues
  under the per-server advisory lock in `lib/job-guard.ts`.
  **Slow-start rule (2026-10-02, Valheim "terraheim" false FAILED restarts).** A start/restart is FAILED
  only when the game process is dead (runtime state crashed / game_stopped / unhealthy, seen twice in a
  row while waiting, so fast-fail) — never merely because the port is not bound yet. `lib/game-power-start.ts`
  holds the logic: `startWindowMs(spec)` (spec `powerStartTimeoutMs`, else a small family table, else 30 s)
  and `runPowerStartCheck`. If the window ends with the unit active and the game not dead, the job ends
  DONE with a "<Game> is starting" notification and the runtime badge shows **Starting** (no red failure).
  `gamePower` in `lib/actions-game-control.ts` refuses a repeat Start/Restart while a fresh `starting`
  runtime reading is within the 6-minute grace (the in-flight job guard already covered queued/running
  jobs). `lib/power-state.ts` now also maps the worker's "never answered" wording (previously only "never
  bound", so it fell through to "we couldn't reach the server"). GAME_REINSTALL and GAME_CONFIG restarts
  use the same per-family window as a floor. Valheim boots ~65-75 s after `docker start` (steamcmd verify
  ~17 s + ~50 s world load); its spec window is 180 s (already on main since 2026-10-01 — if prod still
  shows the 30 s message, the worker running there predates that commit and needs a promote).
- **Live console** — tails `journalctl`/`*.log` over SSH (inline read) and a command box that speaks
  **Source RCON** to `127.0.0.1:<rcon port>` on the VM **through the SSH connection** (`conn.forwardOut`),

# Part VII — Change history

Everything below this line is **history**, not reference. It is kept because the *reasons* recorded in
these entries are often the only surviving explanation for why a piece of code looks the way it does.
Where an entry contradicts Parts I–VI, **Parts I–VI win** — they were verified against the tree; these
were written at the time.

## How to read the change history

```
 Part VII is ordered oldest → newest in three layers:
   1. "Change history — the first 28 commits"   the compressed early record
   2. dated / titled entries                    one H2 per shipped change
   3. "Session log — 2026-07-26/27"             the most recent waves
 Authoritative alternatives when an entry looks stale:
   git log --date=short --pretty='%h|%ad|%s'
   git blame <file> -L <start>,<end>
```

- **2026-10-06 — Automated Reports (/admin/reports).** Deterministic, LLM-free analyst report for any time frame: SQL aggregation across 12 domains, a rule engine with significance tests and 22 friction rules (from the hand-run signup-friction analysis), drill-downs, per-customer journey, CSV (emails masked), print/PDF, saved views, snapshots and an optional (default-off) digest email. Adds ErrorDaily, HttpErrorDaily, ReportView, ReportRun + additive indexes. See "Automated Reports" near the end of this document.

## Session log — 2026-07-26 into 2026-07-27 (the customer-readiness push)

Seven commits, newest first. This document was last verified at `4ea9790`; everything above it in this
table is what the current pass folded in.

| Commit | Subject | Verified state |
|---|---|---|
| `2d8fedd` | Game servers renew at their game-plan price, not the base VPS plan | **Real.** `renewalQuote` delegates to `renewalCharge` and owns no arithmetic; a test asserts the file contains none. The extraction of `lib/renewal-charge.ts` was forced by a bundling failure (`Can't resolve 'fs'`) that `tsc` could not see |
| `f28f15e` | Refuse truncated Stripe metadata; one quote per order; honest receipt | **Real.** `packMetadata` throws before `checkout.sessions.create`; the sold price rides in metadata; the receipt attaches an invoice or points at billing history, never promises one it does not send |
| `3aa24d7` | Verification gates, auth lockouts, email verification (gate ships OFF) | **Mixed by design.** The two auth lockouts and the NAT flush are genuinely fixed. Email verification is **complete and deliberately disarmed** — `email_verification_enforced` defaults to `false` because the platform's DKIM record is missing (gaps 1 and 9). Two of the three agents behind this commit were killed mid-task; what is recorded here is what was verified afterwards, not what was intended |
| `7490131` | Stop charging customers without consent; card-save UI | **Real.** Three launch blockers from `docs/QA-JOURNEY.md`, all reproduced in a browser and all byte-identical in production, plus the card-save UI that had been wrongly marked complete |
| `156b6ac` | Harden the post-cutover TLS sweep against its own first live run | **Real, and verified on the live queue** rather than asserted: jobs drain, the permanent path settles, notifications stopped climbing |
| `4ea9790` | Promo-basis proration, post-cutover TLS, 8 more migration defects | **Real.** `Server.termPromoPercent` makes the proration round trip net zero by construction; the TLS pass stopped being dead code; 4 rows backfilled from real billing records with 0 fallbacks |
| `fd71056` | Migration rehearsal fixes, proration symmetry, wallet floor, CI | **Real.** Nine engine defects, the `capMonths` asymmetry, the sub-Stripe-floor card leg, and the first CI workflow |
